astra-6.text:
I see their role as going beyond simply using a fixed set of tools that we give them. Ideally, the agents should help figure out what tools they need, how to combine them, and how to evaluate whether that workflow is actually working.

For example, you might start with a scientific question, and the agents propose an analysis. As they work through it, they may realize that they need to write some code, bring in another computational tool, or add a validation step. That makes the workflow itself part of the scientific process: propose something, test it, look at the results, and revise.

The important distinction is that creating a workflow doesn't establish that it's scientifically sound. You still need checks grounded in data and, where appropriate, experiments. So I see this as a collaboration: the agents can take on more of the implementation and iteration, while human scientists help define the goals, question the assumptions, and assess whether the results are meaningful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a really interesting role for these agents is to help figure out the workflow itself. You can give the Virtual Lab a high-level scientific goal, but you don’t necessarily want to prescribe every tool or every step. The agents can discuss what approaches might be useful, identify the tools they need, and then write code to connect those tools into a pipeline.

That creates a feedback loop: they run an analysis, look at the results, and decide whether they need to revise the workflow or bring in another method. The human scientist still provides direction and checks the important decisions, but the agents can take on much of the work of assembling and iterating on the computational process. So they’re participating in the design of how to do the science, as well as carrying out individual tasks.
